tips.title: Être plus participle, and it agrees
tips.body: The passive is **être + past participle**, and the participle **agrees with the subject**: *recyclé, recyclée, recyclés, recyclées*. Decide the gender and number of the subject **before** you write the ending, not after.

tips.title: On usually means an English passive
tips.body: *On* rarely translates as *one*. In a general statement it becomes an English **passive** or *they*: *On recycle le verre* is **glass is recycled**. In conversation it usually just means **we**: *On va au cinéma* is *we are going to the cinema*. Decide which from the context, but never write "one recycles".

tips.title: Participle or adjective?
tips.body: *Être* plus a word is only a passive if that word is a **past participle** describing an **action**. *La rivière est sale* is just "the river is dirty" — an adjective, a state, no passive. *La rivière est polluée* is an action done to it.

tips.title: Only être changes for tense
tips.body: To move a passive through the tenses, conjugate **être** alone: *est / a été / était / sera polluée*. The participle never changes for tense, only for the subject. One word to get right instead of two.

steps.title: What the passive does
steps.body:
In an **active** sentence, the subject does the action:

> *Les voitures polluent la ville.* — The cars pollute the town.

In a **passive** sentence, the thing the action happens **to** becomes the subject:

> *La ville **est polluée** par les voitures.* — The town **is polluted** by the cars.

Nothing has changed about the world. What has changed is **what the sentence is about**: the first is about cars, the second about the town.

That is why the passive is everywhere in writing about the environment. Articles are usually about the river, the forest or the town, not about whoever damaged them. And often nobody knows exactly who did it, which the passive lets you leave out entirely:

> *La rivière **est polluée**.* — The river is polluted.

Recognising the passive is a **reading and listening** skill you need; using it accurately is what lifts a piece of **writing** into the top band.

steps.title: How to build it
steps.body:
The passive is two pieces:

$$\textbf{être} + \textbf{past participle}$$

*Être* is conjugated to match the subject, exactly as it is in the perfect tense of *aller* or *partir*. The past participle then **agrees with the subject**.

- masculine singular: no ending — *recyclé*
- feminine singular: add **-e** — *recyclée*
- masculine plural: add **-s** — *recyclés*
- feminine plural: add **-es** — *recyclées*

So:

> *Le verre **est recyclé**.* — Glass is recycled.
> *Les bouteilles **sont recyclées**.* — The bottles are recycled.

The agreement is where marks are won and lost, because it is **audible** in some words and only visible in others. *Recyclée* sounds the same as *recyclé*, but *détruite* does **not** sound like *détruit*: the final **t** is pronounced.

To say **who** did it, add **par**:

> *La forêt est détruite **par les incendies**.*

steps.title: Turning a sentence round
steps.body:
Exam questions often give you an active sentence and ask for the passive, or the other way round. Do it in a fixed order and it is mechanical.

1. Find the **object** of the active sentence: the thing being acted on.
2. Make it the **subject** of your passive sentence.
3. Work out its **gender and number**, because the participle will have to agree.
4. Put **être** in the right person and tense.
5. Add the **past participle**, agreed.
6. If you want to say who did it, add **par** and the old subject.

steps.title: The passive in other tenses
steps.body:
The tense of the passive is carried by **être**, and the participle never changes for tense. So you only have to conjugate one word.

- **Present**: *La rivière **est** polluée.* — The river is polluted.
- **Perfect**: *La rivière **a été** polluée.* — The river **was** polluted, or has been polluted.
- **Imperfect**: *La rivière **était** polluée.* — The river **used to be** polluted, or was polluted (describing a state).
- **Simple future**: *La rivière **sera** polluée.* — The river **will be** polluted.

Notice the perfect: *a été* is *avoir* plus the past participle of *être*. Two participles end up next to each other, and the **second** one is the one that agrees.

> *Les forêts **ont été détruites**.* — The forests have been destroyed.

For writing at the top band, the perfect and future passives are worth having ready, because they let you talk about **what has already been done** and **what will be done** — which is exactly what environmental writing is about.

steps.title: When French avoids the passive
steps.body:
French uses the passive **less** than English does. Two alternatives are extremely common, and recognising them is worth as much as building the passive itself.

**1. On.** French often uses *on* where English uses a passive.

> ***On** recycle le verre ici.* — Glass **is recycled** here. (Literally: one recycles glass here.)
> ***On** a interdit les sacs en plastique.* — Plastic bags **have been banned**.

If you translate *on* as "one", it sounds strange in English. Translate it as a passive, or as "we" or "they", and it sounds natural.

**2. Se + verb**, the reflexive used with a passive meaning.

> *Le verre **se recycle** facilement.* — Glass **is recycled** easily.
> *Ça **se voit**.* — That **can be seen**.

So a reading question can hide a passive idea in an active-looking sentence. If a sentence with *on* or with *se* refuses to make sense translated literally, try it as a passive.

In your own **writing**, using *on* is safer than a passive you are unsure of, and it is not marked down. But a correctly agreed passive shows more range.

steps.title: À toi : the passive in both directions
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Put these into the passive. Watch the agreements.

1. *Les usines polluent la rivière.*
2. *On a planté mille arbres.*
3. *La ville construira une piste cyclable.*

**Partie B.** Translate into natural English.

4. *Les bouteilles sont recyclées dans mon quartier.*
5. *On a interdit les voitures au centre-ville.*
6. *La forêt a été détruite par un incendie.*

**Partie C.** Write two sentences about your own area: one saying what **is** done, and one saying what **has been** done. Use the passive at least once, and *on* at least once.

Check every participle against its subject before you move on. The agreement is the single most common lost mark here.

steps.title: Aller plus loin: using the passive to say more
steps.body:
At the top band the passive is not a grammar trick you insert to show off. It does two jobs that nothing else does as neatly.

**It keeps the topic in the subject position.** If a paragraph is about your town, every sentence starting with the town reads as one connected argument rather than a list. Compare:

> *Les voitures polluent l'air. Les gens jettent des déchets dans la rue. La mairie a fermé le parc.*

Three different subjects, three disconnected facts. Now:

> *Ma ville **est polluée** par les voitures, les rues **sont couvertes** de déchets, et le parc **a été fermé** l'année dernière.*

One topic, three tenses, and it reads as an argument.

**It lets you avoid blaming anyone.** Sometimes you genuinely do not know who is responsible, and sometimes saying so is beside the point:

> *Beaucoup d'arbres **ont été coupés**.* — A lot of trees have been cut down.

Two cautions worth carrying into the exam.

- **Do not overuse it.** Three passives in a row reads as translated English. French prefers *on* in speech, so a spoken answer full of passives sounds unnatural.
- **Agreement is not optional.** A passive with the wrong ending is worse than an active sentence that is right, because it draws attention to exactly the thing that is wrong.

And one thing that sounds like a passive and is not: *être* plus an adjective. *La rivière est sale* is simply "the river is dirty" — an adjective, not a participle, and no action at all.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- The **passive** makes the thing acted on into the **subject**: *La ville est polluée.*
- Build it with **être + past participle**.
- The participle **agrees with the subject**: *recyclé, recyclée, recyclés, recyclées*.
- Add **par** to say who did it: *détruite **par** les incendies*.
- The **tense is carried by être**: *est* / *a été* / *était* / *sera* polluée.
- In the perfect, two participles meet — ***ont été détruites*** — and the **second** one agrees.
- French often prefers **on**: *On recycle le verre* means **glass is recycled**, and should be translated as a passive.
- **Se + verb** can also carry a passive meaning: *Le verre se recycle facilement.*
- Translating *on* as "one" reads as an error in English.
- The passive keeps a paragraph **about one topic**, which makes writing read as an argument.
- **Être + adjective** is not a passive: *La rivière est sale* is just "the river is dirty".
- Wrong agreement is worse than not using the passive at all.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

> *Ma ville **est polluée** par les voitures, surtout le matin quand tout le monde va au travail. L'année dernière, beaucoup d'arbres **ont été coupés** près de la gare, ce que je trouve vraiment dommage. Heureusement, le verre et le papier **sont recyclés** dans mon quartier depuis deux ans. L'année prochaine, une nouvelle piste cyclable **sera construite**, et j'espère que moins de gens prendront la voiture.*

**What earns the marks.** Four passives across **four tenses**: present (*est polluée*, *sont recyclés*), perfect (*ont été coupés*), future (*sera construite*). Every participle agrees: *polluée* feminine singular, *coupés* masculine plural, *recyclés* masculine plural, *construite* feminine singular.

The opinions (*ce que je trouve vraiment dommage*, *j'espère que*) are what lift it above a list of facts.

Renders *on a interdit* naturally, as a passive or with 'they', never as 'one'

questions.modelAnswer:
**Traduction.**

> In my area, glass **has been recycled** for a long time. Plastic bags **were banned** last year, and a lot of trees **have been planted** in the park.

**Three things to notice.**

- ***Est recyclé depuis longtemps***. French uses the **present** with *depuis*; English needs **has been recycled**. A literal "is recycled for a long time" is wrong in English.
- ***On a interdit***. Translate as a **passive** — *were banned* — or with *they*. **Never "one has banned"**, which reads as an error.
- ***Ont été plantés*** is the perfect passive: **have been planted**.

examTechnique.body:
In **reading and listening**, the passive is a recognition skill. *Être* plus a participle means something is being done **to** the subject, and *par* tells you by whom. Do not confuse it with *être* plus an adjective.

When you **translate into English**, look out for *on* and for *se* plus a verb. Both usually become English passives, and a literal translation of *on* as "one" costs the mark.

When you **write**, decide the gender and number of the subject before you write the participle. Say the sentence in your head: in *détruite* and *construite* the final **t** is pronounced, which is a useful check.

To move a passive into another tense, change **être** and leave the participle alone.

Use the passive to keep a paragraph about one topic, but do not stack three in a row. In speaking, *on* sounds more natural than a string of passives.
examinerErrors: Forgetting the agreement, so *la forêt est détruit* instead of *détruite*.
Using *avoir* instead of *être* to build the passive.
Translating *on* as 'one', which reads as an error in English.
Treating *être* plus an adjective as a passive: *la rivière est sale* is not one.
Agreeing *été* rather than the second participle in *ont été détruites*.
Changing the participle to show tense instead of conjugating *être*.
Using *pour* or *avec* for the agent, where *par* is wanted. A few set expressions do take *de*, such as *couvert de*.
Filling a spoken answer with passives, where French would use *on*.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer uses the passive because it does something, not to show it can: it keeps a paragraph about the town or the river so the writing reads as a connected argument rather than a list of facts. It moves the passive through tenses confidently, changing only *être*, and every participle agrees. In translation it recognises *on* and *se* as passive in meaning and renders them in natural English rather than word by word. It also knows when **not** to use the passive: in speech, and where an adjective is what is really wanted.
